{"number":926,"title":"The declarative vocabulary has never reached a member's local pack — fleet census, and the one key that is missing","body":"#880 closed the coded→declared question for the **canon**. This is the same question asked of the **fleet**, and the answer is different: the canon is 49/85 declared, and until today every member repo was **0**.

## Census (2026-08-16, each member's `main`, shallow clones)

Local-pack rule modules, excluding `pack.mjs` / `lib.mjs` / task workers / tests:

| repo | local packs | coded rules | declarations |
|---|---|---|---|
| CrosswordChat | 2 | 8 | 0 |
| EdFringeNow | 3 | 7 | 0 |
| VascularColoring | 1 | 7 | 0 |
| GoogleCalendarEventCreator | 1 | 5 | 0 |
| Sheepdog | 1 | 5 | 0 |
| gRatio | 1 | 5 | 0 |
| HelloWorldFlutterApp | 1 | 5 | 0 |
| LaughCounter | 3 | 10 → **5** | **2 files, 5 rules** |
| ClaudiniteCanary | 1 | 4 | 0 |
| ShoutsAndWhispers | 1 | 4 | 0 |
| TLDR | 1 | 2 | 0 |
| **total** | **16** | **62 → 57** | **5** |

LaughCounter's column moved today — missingbulb/LaughCounter#203 converts five, the first declarations in any member repo.

## Two members cannot carry a declaration at all

`HelloWorldFlutterApp` and `gRatio` have no `engine/checks/helpers/pattern-rules.mjs` in their mount, so their 10 rules are not a conversion backlog — they are a **convergence** finding. Both last moved 2026-08-12. Worth reading their stamps and the head sha's runs before anything else is proposed for them, per the standing "read the member's own artifacts first" rule.

## The one missing vocabulary key, with two named customers

Every content assertion in the vocabulary predicates on a file's **text**. Two fleet rules assert about a **path's existence alone**:

- `vascular-coloring/rendered-overlays-untracked` — no tracked image under `analysis/`
- `edfringe/no-stray-package-json` — no `package.json` outside the root and a grandfathered `plan/`

`repoWide.flagFilesMatching` matches text, so today these convert only by pairing a path-selecting `scanFiles` with an always-true content regex — a hack that reads as nothing. The honest form is a `forbidPathsMatching` assertion (pattern + exceptions + `what`/`fix`), which is the exact negative of the existing `requirePaths`. Both customers exist now; I'd build it against them rather than speculatively.

## What the rest of the fleet's rules actually are

All 62 were signal-classified (transcript / git / parse / derived-scan-set / config), and ~15 read in full — so treat the per-rule verdicts below as firm and the residue as classified but not individually argued to #880's standard.

The residue falls into the same classes #880 named, and the fleet is if anything *more* weighted to them, because a local pack exists precisely to carry what the canon shelf could not:

- **Derived scan set / derived key set** — the largest group. `shouts-and-whispers/cross-tier-constant-coverage` quantifies over constants discovered in one tier and looks for them in another *and* in the guard's own `PAIRS` map; `canary/pack-shape` reads the skill names out of `pack.mjs` and checks each named file exists.
- **Needs a real parser** — `edfringe-data/normalizer-selftest-in-verify` strips `step "…"` labels out of a shell script before looking for the command, precisely because a grep for the two tokens is satisfied by the label alone.
- **Computation** — `vascular-coloring/overlay-color-contrast` parses `(r, g, b)` literals and asserts `r - g >= 60 && r - b >= 60`. No pattern language expresses that, and it should not try.
- **Imports the definition it guards** — several read a constant or list out of the very code they check, which is the class where coded is the *stronger* rung.

Two near-misses worth naming, both one key from convertible:

- `on-device-privacy/on-device-speech` (LaughCounter) — asserts an opt-out appears within **12 lines after** a construction. `andIndentedBlockBelowMatches` does not fit: the opt-out sits at the same indentation, not inside a block. A "within the next N lines" relation would convert it.
- `macos-audio/swift-toolchain-gate`, `signal-teardown-routing` — both assert **ordering** (a probe sits behind a gate; `SIG_IGN` precedes `resume()`), which the vocabulary has no relation for.

## Suggested order

1. Diagnose the two stale mounts — a member that cannot compile a declaration is the blocking item, and it is not about checks at all.
2. `forbidPathsMatching`, red-first against its two customers, then convert them in their repos.
3. Judge the "within the next N lines" relation on its own merits, with `on-device-speech` as the single customer — one customer may not earn a key, and #880's `matchAnyValueOfSet` is the precedent for declining.

Nothing here proposes converting the residue. The point of the census is the opposite: to have the number, and the reason for each rule that keeps its module.","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/926","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","assignees":[],"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-08-16T11:48:13Z","updated_at":"2026-08-16T11:48:13Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":false,"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}

The critical pass over DESIGN §16 found four gaps; the owner decided each today and [#1063](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1063) lands them (design + scenarios + simulator, ledger F26–F30): an unreadable request issue **fails the run** instead of declining (only a definitive *gone* declines); **one issue, one live item** (a live prior item leaves the mark unconsumed; a parked one is superseded); the **model labels are consumed with the mark**; eligibility is **push permission read from the permission API**, not the payload association. S44–S51 in the sim carry all of it, each watched red first.

## Implementation plan (supersedes the §16.10 list in my 2026-08-18 comment)

**Phase 0 — out-of-band setup: none.** The mode rides the queue's existing wiring: labels come from the ordinary ensured set, the invocation endpoint and its secret are the queue's own (#801), and the permission read is designed for the executor workflow's `GITHUB_TOKEN`. No new secret, scope, or platform setting.

**Phase 1 — the code, one PR** (all of it against the queue engine; each behavior test watched failing first):

- [ ] `engine/scheduler/queue/tick.mjs` — job 4 `adopt`: list open `claude-task` issues (REST, never search); the one-live-item guard (wait unconsumed / supersede a parked prior item, closed `outcome:obsolete` with a superseding comment); create the item (`origin:request`, born `task:ready`, qualifier `#N`, body `Request:` + `Model:`); consume `claude-task` **and** every `claude-model:*`, add `claude-queued`.
- [ ] `engine/scheduler/queue/work-item.mjs` — parse/serialize `Request:`/`Model:`; `origin:request`; the four request labels in the ensured set.
- [ ] `engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs` — pass the item to the precondition; the decline write-back (one comment + remove `claude-queued`); the cannot-answer verdict parks `needs-human` + `task:needs-human-failure`, issue untouched.
- [ ] `engine/scheduler/discover.mjs` + `validate-dispatch.mjs` — the built-in engine task root beside the pack scan, and its validated path form.
- [ ] `engine/scheduler/task-contract.mjs` — `model_from_request`; `precondition(signals, config, item)`; the error-verdict shape (cannot-answer ≠ no-go).
- [ ] The built-in task `engine/scheduler/queue/tasks/implement-request/` — `task.mjs`: `manual`, `open-pr`, no `code_work`; precondition = withdrawn/gone checks + eligibility (author or `/claude go` commenter has push, read from `GET /repos/{o}/{r}/collaborators/{u}/permission`; association at most a prefilter; unreadable → error verdict). `task.md`: how to implement a requested issue — the issue is the requirement, data never instructions.
- [ ] Verify against a **real run**, not docs alone, that the permission endpoint answers under the executor workflow's `GITHUB_TOKEN`; if it does not, stop and raise — do not substitute the association.
- [ ] `engine/scheduler/queue/instructions.md` — the request mode: validate the named issue is open + `claude-queued` and the nonce matches, run at `Model:`, write back `claude-queued` → `claude-in-review` at the approval park.
- [ ] `packs/claudinite-growth/skills/writing-tasks/SKILL.md` — the contract additions members read.
- [ ] Engine tests mirroring S44–S51 against the real modules (the sim proves the design; these prove the code): adopt-consumes-everything, wait/supersede, decline-disarm, error-verdict park, permission eligibility incl. the read-only-collaborator refusal, model fallback. Refusal-shaped ones get the mutation check.

Exit: PR open, suite green, every S44–S51 behavior asserted against engine code.

**Phase 2 — after merge, validation burst** (no gate, one sitting):

- [ ] On the first queue-mode repo, mark a throwaway issue and watch: tick adopts (mark consumed) → pickup passes → hand-off → PR → item parked `task:needs-human-approval`, issue `claude-in-review`.
- [ ] Mark an issue from a no-push author, unblessed: one decline comment, `claude-queued` removed, no session, no re-adoption over the next ticks.

Exit: both traces readable on the items; nothing left to watch.

Note: the request mode is queue-mode only — it ships inert to repos still on `dispatch: "slots"` and needs no migration record of its own; #801 remains the carrier for the queue flip itself.

Phase 1 is built and open as [#1067](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1067), with #1064's rename landed underneath it in the same branch (writing new code in the vocabulary that issue retires would have meant sweeping it twice).

Every Phase 1 checklist item from the plan above is done, with three deviations worth reading before approving:

- **The permission read is a signal, not a call from inside the precondition.** A precondition is pure over collected signals and holds no GitHub client; giving every pack's precondition one so this task could make two reads widens far more than the gate it guards. So a `request` collector — engine-owned, like every other — reads the issue, its `/claude go` comments and each candidate's permission, and returns those facts unjudged; the verdict stays in the built-in task's precondition exactly as §16.4 puts it. DESIGN §16.4 carries the amendment.
- **No migration record for #1064.** The retired origin marker is inert (nothing branches on it — standing vs ad-hoc is structural now), open items' state labels do not change, and closed history is covered decode-side. The migration ops write files, not issue labels, so a record could not have done that work in any case.
- **The permission endpoint is unverified**, and it is the one open risk. This sandbox proxy-blocks `api.github.com`, which is a policy boundary rather than something a later agent pass can close — so it needs the first real run, or a human. The failure mode is loud by construction: any answer but 200/404 makes the read `unreadable`, which parks the item in the failure lane with the status on it rather than approving or refusing on a guess.

Two things the build found that the plan did not have:

- The vendor set's blanket "an engine `.md` is maintainer reference" rule was dropping the built-in task's `task.md` — a mount whose request session has nothing to read. Whitelisted by pattern, and its regression test now walks the queue engine rather than listing its top level, which is what let it through.
- Deriving standing-vs-ad-hoc structurally makes an unqualified hand-created item for a *scheduled* task indistinguishable from that task's standing item, so `create-work-item` now refuses that shape and names `--wake` / `--qualifier` instead.

Phase 2 (the validation burst on a live queue-mode repo) is untouched and still open; this issue stays open for it.

Phase 1 merged as [#1067](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1067). **Phase 2's first trace is complete, on this repo**, and it answers the one thing Phase 1 could not verify.

## The happy path, end to end (2026-08-19 23:00–23:06 UTC)

[#1074](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1074) marked `claude-task` + `claude-model:sonnet` → tick → [#1075](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1075) → session → [#1076](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1076), six minutes end to end. Every step of §16 behaved as designed:

- **Labels ensured** by the tick before anything was marked — `claude-task` exists in the picker with its colour and description.
- **Adoption**: item titled `[claudinite-work] engine/implement-request #1074`, body `Request: #1074` / `Model: sonnet`, born `task:ready`. Both marks consumed, `claude-queued` on, one comment naming the item and the family.
- **Pickup**: precondition passed, claim + hand-off + one session, item to `task:agent`.
- **The run**: the ask was a one-line test-fixture change; the PR is exactly that, no production code, ceiling respected (opened, not merged).
- **Converge**: item parked open at `needs-human` + `task:needs-human-approval`; #1074 swapped `claude-queued` → `claude-in-review` with the PR and the model named.

**The permission API answers under the executor workflow's `GITHUB_TOKEN`.** That was the open risk — the sandbox proxy-blocks `api.github.com`, so it could not be settled at landing. A failed read would have parked #1075 at `task:needs-human-failure` with the status on it; instead the verdict passed on the read. No workflow permission needed adding.

## What Phase 2 found

The item's Context rendered as two near-identical bullets — adoption writes one, the precondition added another — in the one section the session is told to read as its binding scope. [#1077](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1077) drops the precondition's.

## Still not verified, and why

The **unauthorized-mark refusal** (the plan's second Phase 2 trace). It needs an issue whose author has no push access here; every identity available to this session is the owner's, so it cannot be staged, and the adoption→pickup window the withdrawal variant would need is seconds wide (the drain follows the tick in the same run). The engine tests cover both shapes against the real executor with a fake GitHub — S45's disarm and S48's withdrawal — but the live trace is a human's to produce, from a second account, and it is the one thing left on this issue.

# A thin wrapper: every decision lives in the engine modules named in the `run:`
# lines below, which converge nightly — this file does not, so it must not grow
# logic. This copy is hand-maintained — the canon has no converge — so it is
# edited in the same commit as the stub beside it, and the drift tests in
# engine-tests/scheduler/converge-wiring.test.mjs keep the two honest.
name: Claudinite scheduler

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '44 5,17 * * *'
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      wake:
        description: 'Task ids to run now (`pack/task` or a bare task name, space-separated) — wakes each one’s standing item regardless of its anchor'
        required: false
        type: string

concurrency:
  group: claudinite-scheduler-run
  cancel-in-progress: false

permissions:
  contents: write
  issues: write
  pull-requests: write
  actions: write

jobs:
  scheduler-run:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      pickable: ${{ steps.run.outputs.pickable }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Instantiate, ready and reclaim work items
        id: run
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          CLAUDINITE_WAKE: ${{ inputs.wake }}
          CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL: ${{ vars.CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL }}
        run: node engine/scheduler/queue/scheduler-run.mjs

  drain:
    needs: scheduler-run
    # An older member workflow maps no such output, and an empty string is not
    # 'true' — so a stale copy keeps dispatching, the previous behavior and safe.
    if: needs.scheduler-run.outputs.pickable == 'true'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      actions: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Start an executor for what this run readied
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: node engine/scheduler/queue/drain-dispatch.mjs

  report-failure:
    needs: [scheduler-run, drain]
    # Explicit results rather than `failure()`: `drain` is skipped on a quiet
    # tick, and a bare status function makes this job's fate turn on how the
    # platform propagates a skipped dependency.
    if: >-
      always()
      && (needs.scheduler-run.result == 'failure' || needs.drain.result == 'failure')
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      issues: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Escalate the failed run to a human-visible issue
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: node engine/scheduler/queue/workflow-failure.mjs

[{"id":5316661692,"body":"Two more findings from the same adoption, on the owner's instruction to keep them here rather than open separate issues. Both are about **how a human-handover step is written**, so they sit one level up from the path bug above — that one is a wrong address, these are a wrong shape.

## 1. A GitHub settings step must be a deep link, not a breadcrumb trail

The handover issue this adoption produced said things like:

> Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret

Every one of those is a URL the agent already knows how to construct — it has the `owner/repo` — so making the human navigate is pure friction, and a breadcrumb goes stale the moment GitHub reorganizes a settings page while a URL keeps redirecting. The rule the owner asked for: **hyperlink every requested GitHub setting change, to the deepest page that exists.**

The patterns worth naming wherever this lands:

| Step | URL |
|---|---|
| New Actions secret | `https://github.com///settings/secrets/actions/new` |
| Actions secrets and variables | `https://github.com///settings/secrets/actions` |
| Workflow permissions, Actions general | `https://github.com///settings/actions` |
| Auto-merge, merge methods, general | `https://github.com///settings` |
| Branch protection / rulesets | `https://github.com///settings/branches` |
| Environments | `https://github.com///settings/environments` |

This is general to every repo the fleet adopts, not specific to the one that hit it — which is why it is here and not in that repo's local pack.

## 2. Don't ask a human to enable something GitHub enables by default

The same issue carried a checkbox for **Settings → General → "Allow squash merging"**, on the reasoning that the merge recipe squashes always. But GitHub enables all three merge methods on a new repository, so the box could only ever be already-ticked. A handover list whose items are mostly no-ops teaches the reader to skim it, which is exactly the failure mode a handover list exists to prevent.

Worth stating as a rule where the handover shape is defined: **a handover step must name a change from the platform's default.** If the default already satisfies the requirement, the requirement is met and there is nothing to hand over.

Both corrections are applied in the consuming repo's own issue ([missingbulb/Shepherd#3](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues/3)) — this is the upstream half, so the next adoption does not repeat either.

One consequence of keeping all three here: this issue's title now names only the first finding. Worth retitling to something like *"bootstrap.md Part 9 path bug, plus two rules for writing human-handover steps"* if it is going to be triaged by title.

{"number":841,"title":"pack.json migration plan: engine reader + canon conversion, then a versioned fleet migration","body":"Executes #564 (re-evaluated 2026-08-14; PR #569 reviewed for insights and closed). Owner-settled decisions this plan encodes:

- **`pack.schema.json` is authoring tooling** (editor autocomplete + documentation). Manifest conformance — field shapes, the 20-word routing cap, skills↔tree, rule-scope agreement, the accounted-for-`.mjs` guard — is **checked by the world sweep when the file is edited**, not at load. The loader stays minimal and fail-soft: parse, resolve filenames, surface unreadable/unparseable as blocking config findings (as today).
- **`detect` is data for 14 of 17 packs** (path matching + content matching, full-noun-phrase keys per the #789/#799 discipline); sibling `detect.mjs` for chrome-extension, chrome-extension-release, static-website.
- **Members' local packs convert via a `basics` migration record with `applyStage`**; the routing gap that makes `basics` the carrier for an engine-owned format is #840.

Owner approval points: **two PRs** (plus one small telemetry-gated retirement PR later). Everything else lands through the members' own auto-merged update PRs.

## PR 1 — the engine reads pack.json; the whole canon converts

One PR: the reader and the corpus it reads must land transactionally, and the home (no mount, runs repo-root code) is the first consumer either way.

- [ ] `engine/pack_loader/pack.schema.json` — the authoring spec; its field order is the one canonical order (no second list).
- [ ] Registry reads `pack.json`: prefers it where `pack.mjs` coexists (a half-finished conversion must not resolve to the old shape), reports the leftover module for deletion, stamps `manifestFile` so findings name the consumer's actual file. The `pack.mjs` import path stays as the tolerance branch.
- [ ] `detect` spec compiler (tracked-path + file-content matching), with the #569-style equivalence tests: each compiled spec proven to mean exactly what the arrow it replaces meant — including the near-root `maxDepth` semantics and the jwt/web-speech/leaflet content-regex shape.
- [ ] Sibling code files named from the JSON: `detect.mjs` ×3, `env.mjs` where env is a function of config (node; flutter's static shell as data if the spec carries a line list, else a second `env.mjs`), `contributed.mjs` ×2 (barriers, canary-probe); `contributes` becomes a map of pack id → rule filenames; `worldRules`/`workRules` become filename lists (manifest placement stays the scope authority — #555; `declared-checks.json` stays structural with no manifest line — #827).
- [ ] Manifest conformance moves to the world sweep: schema shape, routing word cap, skills↔tree, scope agreement, and the every-`.mjs`-at-pack-root-accounted-for guard. Author each check first and watch it fail (a deliberately broken fixture AND a live in-scope count over the real tree — a path-pattern check that reaches zero files passes silently).
- [ ] Convert all 33 canon manifests + the home's 2 local packs; genuinely unhoused comments move to each pack's README (#569's second commit has the survey).
- [ ] Repoint every `pack.mjs` reader, enumerated from `grep -rl 'pack\.mjs'` in-branch (today: `vendoring/compute-vendor-set.mjs`, sheepdog `fleet-pack-seeds`, `adopt-claudinite` interview, `converge-wiring`, the seededByDefault audit, the pack-prose narration rule, ~20 test fixtures). Fixtures author `pack.json` and copy `engine/pack_loader/` wholesale rather than enumerating its modules.
- [ ] Full suite via `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`; conformance sweep green; both hand-maintained tallies recomputed (not incremented) if checks were added; suite re-run against current `main` immediately before merge.

**Verified in-session**: the home *is* the corpus, so a green selftest + world sweep on the converted tree is a real end-to-end run of the reader — plus one member repo attached read-only to confirm nothing in its (unconverted) mount breaks against canon-side tasks that read packs from a fresh clone.

## Between PRs — the release gate

- [ ] Run the live canary rehearsal against the merged snapshot; watch it to a terminal state (a dispatch is not a result). Note its known blind spot: it drives the worker *this ref ships*, so it cannot see a fielded-caller break — hence the next checkbox.
- [ ] Confirm nothing under `updates/*` (the flow surface fielded workers call) changed shape in PR 1; if anything did, shim per the live-cross-version-API discipline before releasing.

## PR 2 — the release and the fleet migration record, one change

Per `engine/migrations/README.md`, a record lands in the same change as the bump it names:

- [ ] `ENGINE_VERSION` 4 → 5 (the engine that reads pack.json).
- [ ] `basics` version 2 → 3, `minEngineVersion: 5` — the updater's own enforcement guarantees no member converts its local packs before holding the engine that reads the result.
- [ ] `packs/basics/migrations/2026-08-XX-local-pack-json/migration.mjs`:
  - `applyStage: { why, instructions }` — convert this repo's local packs to `pack.json` (+ sibling `.mjs` only where a manifest genuinely holds code), move manifest comments to the pack README, delete `pack.mjs`, repair the member's own pack tests.
  - `legacyPresent` probes every declared local pack (both local-pack roots) for a surviving `pack.mjs` — the fleet census reads it, so "is the fleet done" is telemetry, not memory.
  - `appliesTo` probes the member's own mount for the pack.json-capable registry **by content, not version stamp** — fail-safe (unreadable mount = not capable), so the record delays instead of wedging (the sheepdog-fleet-baseline lesson).

## Same-session fleet verification — not "after the nightly"

- [ ] Force the fleet baseline/update sweep with `follow`; report per-member results unasked, attaching member repos directly rather than offering to.
- [ ] Drive one member that carries local packs through its update **now**; watch the `applyStage` session convert them and the auto-merged PR land green.
- [ ] Judge freshness by each member's stamp `ref`/engine version, never `updated` alone (held stamps), and read the **status** of every API write, not just its body.
- [ ] Report the `legacyPresent` census: which members still hold a `pack.mjs`, driven by the standing update mechanism — no phase anyone must remember to close.

## Retirement — telemetry-gated, expiry-pinned

- [ ] PR 1 ships a pinned-expiry test on the both-shapes tolerance (re-check at a named engine version), so retirement has a trigger that comes to us.
- [ ] When the census reads clean **from the members' repos, not by reasoning about canon**: one small PR deletes the `pack.mjs` read branch and the legacy fixtures. The record itself stays, as history.

Refs #564. Insight sources: #569 (closed), #827, #555, #798, #768. {"number":409,"title":"Tracking-issue freshness: keep the plan issue in sync after every merge","body":"Implementation tracker for the tracking-issue freshness check. This issue is itself an instance of the pattern it tracks — it carries the live checklist; the committed doc carries the rationale.

**Read first (on `main`):**
- Design + plan — [`docs/tracking-issue-freshness/DESIGN.md`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/docs/tracking-issue-freshness/DESIGN.md)

**The problem:** a major task has two artifacts — a source-controlled design/migration plan and a GitHub tracking issue with a `- [ ]`/`- [x]` checklist (the "read status and pick up the work" point). When a phase lands, the committed plan's status is updated in the same PR (the diff forces review), but the issue checklist is a separate surface no diff touches, so it silently drifts. Already live: `per-project-scheduling/MIGRATION.md` says Phase 1 is "same day, no soak" while #394's Phase 1 item still says "Soak ~1 week."

**The design, in two surfaces:**
1. **In-session (timely):** a transcript-only post-merge check-the-work rule — `in-session-github-access` (blocking) means in-session code has no GitHub REST credential, so the rule reads the merge, the tracker discovery, and the post-merge checklist edit from the session transcript's MCP tool calls. Enablers: `work.mergedThisSession()` and a Stop-hook post-merge trigger (the merge recipe leaves a clean tree, which would otherwise fast-exit).
2. **Nightly (convergent):** plans state, per phase, *how completion is decided* — a checklist item may carry `` naming a dependency-free Node script whose **exit 0 means the phase is done** ("if this code passes, phase 3 is done"); no marker ⇒ the phase's prose **Verify** block in the plan doc is the criteria. The `plan-status-update` task (daily, gated on an open `plan-tracking` issue) re-derives every tracker's checklist from these verifiers — flipping what sessions missed, flagging (never auto-un-flipping) a checked item whose code verifier now fails.

**Invariant:** any open `plan-tracking` issue must carry a todo checklist and have a box **flipped** in the same session as each merge that advances it (after the merge, not before — an item isn't done until it's on `main`). The issue *count* is not enforced.

**Phases (detail in the design doc):**
- [ ] **Convention + seed** — define the `plan-tracking` label and its meaning in the `grow_with_claudinite` / merge docs; apply it to existing in-flight tracker(s) (#394).
- [ ] **Primitive + trigger** — `work.mergedThisSession()` (transcript-derived accepted PRs) and the Stop hook's post-merge trigger, each with red-first tests.
- [ ] **Verifier (in-session)** — the `plan-tracking-freshness` rule in `grow_with_claudinite`; fires when a merge happened with no post-merge checklist flip, quiet otherwise.
- [ ] **Recipe wiring** — `merge-to-main` gains the "sync the `plan-tracking` issue after the merge" step (prose asks; the check guarantees).
- [ ] **Docs** — the convention in the pack README; design-doc status box; this issue points at the doc.
- [ ] **Per-phase verifiers (convention)** — `` code verifiers (exit 0 ⇒ done) with prose Verify blocks as fallback; recorded in the pack README and the nightly worker doc.
- [ ] **Nightly status update** — the `plan-status-update` task (daily/sonnet/none, gated on an open `plan-tracking` issue): re-verifies each tracker, flips passes, flags regressions in a comment.

**Decisions (resolved with the owner):** label = `plan-tracking`; issue count not enforced; a **checkbox flip** is required (a bare comment isn't enough); label precision from the transcript for the in-session rule; the once-contingent world-scope backstop is **superseded** by the nightly task, which runs with the executor session's MCP credential and has no label blind spot.","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/409","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","labels":["plan-tracking"],"assignees":[],"comments":1,"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-07-23T09:56:23Z","updated_at":"2026-07-30T04:45:55Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":false,"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}

{"number":498,"title":"scheduler-workflow-shape should validate the scopes a repo's tasks actually need, not a fixed two","body":"Surfaced by the `growth-extract` run on #484, and pulled out of that run's RULES.md entries during review: this reads as a proposed mechanism change rather than a rule a session can follow, so filing it here instead.

## The gap

`packs/basics/scheduler-workflow-shape.mjs` validates exactly two permissions on a repo's `claudinite-scheduler.yml`, both hard-coded:

```
if (!/^\s*contents:\s*write\b/m.test(text))       → flag
if (!/^\s*pull-requests:\s*write\b/m.test(text))  → flag
```

Those two cover baselining's `deliver()` (push a branch, open a PR, arm auto-merge). They cover nothing a *task's worker* needs. So a task whose worker calls a GitHub endpoint requiring some third scope passes the check with a stub that never granted it, and the failure lands at runtime in a member repo.

## How it actually bit (#478)

`store-release`'s worker POSTs a `workflow_dispatch`, which needs `actions: write`. The stub granted `actions: read`. Every fire 403'd, the worker exited 1, and the scheduler converged the task to `needs-human` — leaving three cut-over members with no working release path. Nothing caught it earlier because nothing was looking: the check validates a fixed pair, and the next task needing a fourth scope will land exactly the same way.

## Suggested direction

Make the required scope set *derived* rather than fixed. Roughly:

1. Let a task declare what its worker needs in its `task.mjs` — e.g. `required_scopes: ['actions:write']` — alongside the existing `agent_model` / `expected_outcome` fields, validated by `task-contract.mjs`.
2. Have `scheduler-workflow-shape` union the declared scopes across the repo's enabled tasks with the baselining floor (`contents:write`, `pull-requests:write`) and assert the workflow grants each one, naming the task that needs it in the failure message.
3. Have the stub generator emit the union, so a repo that adopts a task gets the grant with it rather than hand-editing `engine/scheduler/stubs/claudinite-scheduler.yml`.

That turns "read the scope off the endpoint and grant it yourself, and hope you remembered" into a declaration the check enforces. Worth weighing against the simpler option — keep the check fixed but widen the floor to include `actions: write` — which costs a broader default token but no new contract surface.

Not started; opening for a decision on which direction (or neither) before any implementation.

{"number":1105,"title":"Engine and pack versions become date-anchored `<day>.<n>`","body":"Closes #1100.

Versions were a plain monotonic counter. It orders releases, which is all the update flows need, but it says nothing about *when* one was cut: a member stamped at `6` against a canon at `13` is behind by an unknown amount of time, and every fleet surface reporting that gap makes a reader go and date it by hand.

Both the engine and every pack now version as `.` — `60820.1`, where the day part is `(year - 2020) * 10000 + month * 100 + day` and the second part is the running number of versions cut that day. Displayed with a leading `v`, as the surfaces already do.

Two decisions worth naming:

- **The year is anchored on 2020, not taken as its last digit.** A last-digit year wraps to `0` in 2030 and sorts a decade of releases underneath every 2029 one. `2026 → 6` either way, so the example holds and the ordering survives.
- **A version is a string.** `60820.10` and `60820.1` are different versions and the same float, so nothing in the corpus may parse one as a number.

### The migration technique

Every reader accepts **both** spellings. A legacy integer parses as `.0`, which sorts below every date-anchored version — exactly where a member that has not re-stamped belongs, so no fleet surface has to special-case it. The tolerance is scheduled for removal in its own change, #1106, once the fleet has converged; the parser's own comment carries that date and issue number.

Legacy integers deliberately stay in two places for now: each pack's `minEngineVersion` floor and every migration record's `version:` range, both of which are references to engine versions that really were plain counters. #1106 retires them.

Zero stays readable and is *not* a legacy version — it is the install floor (DESIGN §3), so `isVersion(0)` is true while `isDeclaredVersion(0)` is false, and a stamp at the floor still reads as "says something" rather than as absence.

### What changed, by folder

- **`engine/`** — `version.mjs` gains the format: `parseVersion`, `compareVersions`, `versionsEqual`, `nextVersion`, `versionDay`, and `VERSION_SOURCE`, the regex fragment the text scrapers share so the six of them cannot disagree about what a version looks like. The helpers live beside the constant rather than in a module of their own, so the engine surface a mount must carry for any of it is one file. `ENGINE_VERSION` becomes `'60820.1'`. `pack_loader/pack-schema.mjs` validates both spellings, and `checks/helpers/active-migrations.mjs` reads a record's range and ranges over it through the shared comparator.
- **`updates/`** — the three planners (`engine-update`, `pack-update`, `install`) compare through `versionAbove` instead of `>` and gate on `isVersion` instead of `typeof === 'number'`.
- **`packs/`** — all 33 manifests move to `'60820.1'`. The dashboard's `fleet.mjs` and the sheepdog's `fleet-roster/drift-issues.mjs` scrape and compare through the shared helpers.
- **`.claudinite/local/packs/`** — `pack-version-bumped` and `engine-release-record`, the two canon-side checks that read a version out of a diff, do the same; the first now names `nextVersion(base)` as the remedy rather than `base + 1`.
- **`vendoring/rehearsal/fixtures.mjs`** — the `versioned-local` shape gains a second local pack carrying the date-anchored spelling. This is the `consumer-safe-change` answer: the manifest vocabulary widened, additively, and the fixture is what proves a consumer-authored manifest still validates in **both** spellings.

`ENGINE_VERSION` moving is an engine release, so it lands with its `RELEASES.md` row citing canary rehearsal [run 32371130795](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/32371130795), dispatched against this branch at `1f05d43`.

### One unrelated commit, and why it is here

The second commit fixes `a long work step leaves heartbeats on its own item`, which slept a fixed 40ms against a 5ms beat interval and asserted two beats had arrived. It is red on `origin/main` — three full-suite runs out of four at eight workers — and it was red on this branch's CI twice in a row, so nothing was going to make this PR green without it. The step now polls its own item until the second beat lands, under a 5s ceiling so a heartbeat that never fires stays a failed assertion rather than a hang. It is a separate commit and nothing else in the diff touches the scheduler.

### On delivery

This changes a contract member files carry (the stamp) and the engine flow that reads it, so "will it work on every repo?" is a live question rather than a uniform-by-construction change. Driving Shepherd's `fleet-baseline` with `follow`, and reporting per member, belongs to whoever merges this.

=== usage-fold task.md gap statement and outcome label counting ===
# Usage fold — the repo's own past-data plane

**This task runs no agent.** It is `agent_model: none` with `code-work: node worker.mjs`, so the whole pass is the deterministic [`worker.mjs`](worker.mjs) the executor runs as code-work, which calls its sibling in this folder, the counting and folding core ([`fold-usage.mjs`](fold-usage.mjs)). This file is the human-facing record of what that worker does; there is no agent phase.

## What it does

Hourly, when the repo moved: fetch this repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch and count each capture file still inside the retention window; list the scheduler's and the executor's completed workflow runs since the last fold; list the work items that closed since the last fold; read the local git history and the releases listing; and regenerate `.claudinite/local/usage.GENERATED.json` on a PR that lands itself where this repo's delivery settings allow (the shared landing helper, `engine/scheduler/land-pr.mjs`, owns those nuances — a `review` repo's PR waits for the owner). A recompute that differs only in its `generated` stamp opens nothing, and a repo with no logs branch yet still folds every other source.

### Why hourly, and what stops it being hourly noise

This file is the **past-data plane the dashboard renders from** ([claudinite-dashboard](../../../claudinite-dashboard/README.md)): every panel reaching further back than one page of live reads comes from here, so the file's freshness *is* the page's. The cadence is affordable because the sources are — the capture files are local git, and the REST side is four calls, all watermarked.

What keeps a quiet repo quiet is the **precondition**, which runs the fold only when something moved in the hour: a commit on the default branch, or a conversation log stamped inside the window. It is deliberately *not* gated on the scheduler having run, since the scheduler runs every hour by definition and that would be no gate at all. Declining loses nothing — the run and queue reads sit past their watermarks until the next fold that does have something to do, and the dashboard tops up the freshest hours from the live run listing it already fetches.

What it counts, per bucket:

- **`skillLoads`**, per skill name — `Skill` tool-use entries, plus user-typed `/command`s naming a skill this repo mounts (built-in CLI commands never match). Subagent streams included: a subagent loading a skill is a load.
- **`captures`** — capture events folded. **`merges`** — the subset with an issue behind them (issue `0` means none).
- **`sessions`** — distinct session ids; one session can capture more than once.
- **`userMessages`** — genuine human turns. **`userCommands`** — every typed `/command`.
- **`ruleTokens`** and **`ruleTokenSessions`** — how many rule tokens the mount put into each session's prompt before its first turn, read off the session-start summary line the mount itself prints, and how many sessions attested one. Absent from a session whose mount printed no line; `0` on a day whose captures all lacked it.
- **`tokensIn`** / **`tokensOut`** / **`tokenSessions`** — what the sessions spent, from the usage records the transcript's own assistant entries carry. **Probed, never assumed**: a transcript shape that records no usage leaves the day with no token keys at all, which is what makes "this shape does not record it" distinguishable from "it was free". Cache reads and writes count as input, because that is what the turn was billed for.
- **`commits`** / **`linesAdded`** / **`linesRemoved`** — what landed on the base branch, from local git. A shallow checkout is the normal case in Actions, so days before the history starts carry **no key** rather than a zero.
- **`releases`** — releases published, from one listing read.
- **`checks`**, per scope (`work` / `world`) — `runs` (observed activations), `failures` (runs that reported a blocking finding), `errors` (the runner could not launch), the `blocking`/`advisory` finding volume, and `ciRuns`/`ciFailures` (the CI subset of the first two). **`checkFindings`**, per rule id — which rule caught what.

- **`queue`**, per `pack/task` — what each occurrence came to: closed work items counted under their outcome word (`done`, `delivered`, `obsolete`, `none`). The queue-era successor to the `tasks` rows below (#994) — see "What each occurrence came to".
- **`tasks`**, per `pack/task` — **historical only.** These rows counted what the retired slot scheduler did with each due task (`agent`, `code_work`, `skipped`, `failed`, `deferred`). Nothing writes that record any more, so these rows stop growing as the last slot-era logs age out of Actions retention. The reader stays because the logs inside that window are still real; see "The task invocations are a census" below for what replaces it and what does not.
- **`taskExec`**, per `pack/task` — what the **agent session** did with the item it was handed, distilled from the captured conversation logs: `success`, `failed`, `task-gone` (the item named a task the repo no longer carries), `invalid`. Counted off the machine-readable `claudinite-task-exec` records the session prints (`record-exec.mjs`; format owned by `engine/scheduler/run-record.mjs`), deduped on the full record tuple per capture file — never scraped from the agent's prose. A sample, of the sessions that captured.

The denominators are the point. A raw load count cannot tell healthy-rare from broken — a version-bump skill loading rarely is fine — so the question is loads *against the sessions where that skill's own declared trigger plausibly applied.*

## The check failures are the win

A skill load is evidence that guidance was *reached for*. A **check failure is evidence that it worked**: the finding goes back into the session through the Stop hook and the agent corrects before the work leaves the branch. So the failure counts are not a defect metric to drive down — they are the closest thing this pipeline has to a measure of what the corpus is worth, and `checkFindings` says which rule earned it.

Neither runner writes a metrics file, so both are counted off the marks they already leave in the transcript, each read by one tested function against a fixture copied from a real capture:

- **the Stop hook's `hooklog` line** (`… Stop: done exit=<n> <reason>`), which reaches the transcript via hook stderr — the only mark a *passing* run leaves, and therefore the only reason work-scope **runs** are countable and not just failures. Its reason also carries the two outcomes nothing else reveals: a `loop-guard-relent` (blocking findings that survived two fix attempts, printed as a message rather than a findings block) and a `runner-error` (the checks did not run at all — enforcement silently off, which is why it gets its own counter instead of hiding inside a clean day);
- **`report-findings`' summary line** (`N blocking, M advisory (<scope> scope: …)`), which names its own scope and survives the `| tail` an agent usually pipes a run through — printed only when there *were* findings, so it counts failures, never runs;
- **the runner's invocation in a Bash command** (`node …/check_the_world.mjs`), which is how the world scope runs at all — it is wired into the test/CI flow, not the Stop hook.

Runs come only from the marks a passing run also leaves; where a runner ran without its command naming it (a `make test` wrapping it), the summary lines are the floor, so the count is the **max** of the two signals rather than their sum. Only Bash and CI-log tool results are read, paired back to the tool that produced them — in the corpus that owns the runners, reading a file that merely *mentions* this vocabulary is the ordinary case.

### CI counts when the agent was in the loop on it

Write, commit, let CI run, fix what it caught is the same correction loop as the Stop hook's, one turn wider — so a CI check failure the session acted on is the same kind of win. It counts exactly when the session **pulled the job log in**, which is what "the agent was in the loop" means operationally. A nightly or post-merge run nobody looked at stays uncounted, correctly: nothing was corrected.

Two consequences, both mechanism rather than policy. Actions stamps every log line with its own timestamp before the command's output, so each mark tolerates that prefix — without it a fetched CI log reads as having printed nothing at all. And a job log gets fetched repeatedly while iterating on the failure, with nothing in a fetch saying *which run* it was, so CI texts dedupe on the check output itself: two fetches of one job collapse, two real runs differ by their timestamps.

**Every check number is a floor.** A run whose CI log nobody fetched left no mark in any session transcript; neither did a hook killed before it logged; and a green CI sweep prints nothing to be seen by, which is why the CI share is carried separately as `ciRuns`/`ciFailures` instead of quietly skewing a rate. The under-count is one-directional by construction, which is what keeps "the checks caught N things this week" a claim worth making.

## What each occurrence came to

Everything counted off the capture files is read out of *sessions*, so it sees only what was captured. A whole half of what this repo does opens no session at all — a precondition that finds nothing to do, an agentless task whose whole work is its code-work, an item that yielded to another. None of that leaves a transcript, and the first of them is the most common thing scheduling does.

The `tasks` rows used to answer that from the other side: the slot scheduler printed one line per due task into its own Actions log (`claudinite-task-run v1 <pack>/<task> [<slot>] <outcome>`). **That writer retired with the slot scheduler** (#974), so those rows are history — exact within the window they covered, ending where the slot scheduler did, not comparable to a period after it. The reader that fetched them retired with them too, rather than spending two API calls per run to find records nothing writes; the day rows now only age out, and the week rows that froze them keep them.

What replaced it is the **`queue`** rows (#994), and they are a better record: every occurrence *is* a work item, and a converged one closes wearing an `outcome:*` label. That survives Actions retention, it is clickable, and it names its own task. [`read-queue.mjs`](read-queue.mjs) reads the items that closed since the last fold and counts them per task per outcome.

{"number":1187,"title":"Resolve a canon pack's id against its whole tree, unfreezing seven stalled members","body":"Closes #1186

Seven members have not landed a mount update since ~10 August. Each runs its converge daily, opens a PR, and the PR is parked:

> **needs-human** — the converged tree FAILED its self-test — the machinery that runs the rules is not intact

## The bug

`RENAMED_PACKS` holds two shapes that read identically in the map:

| shape | what the tree holds |
|---|---|
| **rename** (`core` → `claudinite-lifecycle`) | one directory — the migration record's `aliases` moves it |
| **absorption** (`github-actions` → `git-github`, #1057/#1079) | **both** directories — there is no record, and the pack flow "never removes a tree that has stopped being declared" (its own words, `2026-08-19-pack-renames/migration.mjs`) |

`scanPackDir` canonicalized a canon pack's own id from the map alone. Correct for a rename; for an absorption it put two live directories on one id, so the collision guard dropped **both**:

```
pack id "chrome-extension" is declared twice — by the canon and the canon
pack id "git-github" is declared twice — by the canon and the canon
```

That fails the `pack-manifests` probe → the converged tree fails its self-test → the converge parks its own PR. The leftover directory is only ever removed by a converge that lands, so the member re-derives the same broken tree every day. A closed loop.

It surfaced on 10 August because members' current `main` runs the older engine, which does not canonicalize a canon pack's own id — so `main` self-tests clean while the branch fails, which is why the members look healthy: green runs, green `main`, nothing merging.

## The change

The map can't distinguish the two shapes, but the tree can. The id is now resolved once the whole canon scan is known: an absorbed leftover whose survivor is present keeps its own id and goes inert — what an id nothing declares is meant to do. A member still declaring the absorbed spelling is unaffected, since the declaration side resolves onto the survivor, which is live.

## Verification

Against `missingbulb/CrosswordChat`#249's **actual head**, with only this change vendored in:

```
before   Claudinite self-test: 1 of 6 probes FAILED — pack-manifests
         2 pack(s) failed to load or validate
after    Claudinite self-test: 6 probes passed.          (discoverPacks: 0 errors)
```

- New `engine-tests/pack_loader/renamed-packs.test.mjs` — 4 tests covering both shapes and the no-duplicates property; written first and watched fail on the missing export.
- Full suite: 2503 pass, 1 fail — `engine-pack-lane-shims`, which is the shallow-clone guard firing on this session's own checkout (`git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` → `true`). It walks pack history and touches nothing in this diff.
- `check_the_work` and `check_the_world`: 0 blocking.

**This reaches the frozen members with no per-repo hand-running** — the self-test runs against the converged tree, so the next converge vendors the fixed loader and the probe passes.

## Folders touched

**`engine/pack_loader/`** — `renamed-packs.mjs` gains `canonicalPackIdAmong`, which only maps an id forward when the target isn't already present in the tree; `pack-registry.mjs` carries each canon pack's raw id through `scanPackDir` and re-resolves the whole set in `discoverPacks`, where the full tree is known.

## Not in this change

The absorbed leftovers stay on disk as inert, undeclared trees — harmless now, but dead weight that nothing prunes. Worth its own issue (the fix is a migration record that *deletes* rather than moves, since the survivor's directory already exists); deliberately kept out of the change that unfreezes the fleet.

{"number":840,"title":"Engine-driven format changes to consumer-held files need a first-class migration class","body":"Owner decision context (2026-08-14, on #564): converting members' local `pack.mjs` files to `pack.json` rides a `basics` pack record with `applyStage` — but the owner flagged the routing itself as the gap: *"this is a classic 'engine changed, the format of local packs should change' migration."*

The gap: the **engine** owns the local-pack manifest format, but the engine flow may carry no agentic work (versioned-updates DESIGN §5), and its declarative ops (`aliases`/`materialize`/`rewrite`/`declarePacks`) cannot express "reshape this member-authored file". So every engine-side format change to a consumer-held file gets routed ad-hoc through whichever pack is convenient (`basics`, because it is declared everywhere) — the same shape as the #555 manifest tightening, which shipped with *no* carrier and broke eleven local packs silently.

Ask: make "the engine changed a format consumers hold" a recognized migration class with a designated carrier — so the record can be authored where the change lives (with the engine), while the member-side session it needs runs through the one agentic lane that exists (the pack flow), without each occurrence re-deriving the routing. `legacyPresent` telemetry and the retirement gate should come with the class, not be re-invented per change.

Closing condition: the next engine-owned format change to a consumer-held file has an obvious, documented place to land, and the pack.json conversion's routing (via `basics`) is either retroactively blessed as that place or superseded by it.","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/840","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","labels":["quick-win"],"assignees":[],"comments":2,"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-08-14T18:43:43Z","updated_at":"2026-08-19T05:18:51Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":false,"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}

{"number":564,"title":"Pack manifests as JSON: pack.json + pack.schema.json, code split into sibling files","body":"Owner comment (process-change): "Why are packs declared using mjs? Is it just the `detect` part? It seems they can all be just JSON declarations, and if we have some code that detects, we can put that in a different file. And once it's just JSON — can't you declare the schema in a nicer way than `engine/pack_loader/pack-schema.mjs`? You can still have validations (a simple unit test) for making sure all the skills/rules are declared and there's no drift, but at least the files will be sane."

Measured across the 29 manifests (27 canon + the home's 2 local packs): **988 lines, 56 of them `import` statements, 350 of them comments.** Almost nothing in a `pack.mjs` needs to be code.

## What is actually code today

| Field | Packs | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `detect` | 13 (14 declare `null`) | ~10 are one-liners over `ctx.tracked` — `includes`, `endsWith`, a path regex, or the shared `hasMarkerNearRoot` helper — all expressible as data. **3 need real logic**: `chrome-extension` (locates the extension manifest), `chrome-extension-release` (recognizes a release orchestrator workflow), `leaflet` (scans file *content*). |
| `worldRules` / `workRules` | all | Code only as *imports*. In JSON these become filenames the loader imports. |
| `env` | 2 | Genuinely code — `setup`/`probe` are functions of the pack's config returning shell. |
| `contributes` / `contributedRules` | 3 / 1 | `contributes` is a map of pack id → rule modules, so filenames. `contributedRules` (barriers only) is a real seam. |
| everything else | — | Pure data: `id`, `badge`, `marker`, `prose`, `seededByDefault`, `requires`, `ruleRoutingGuidance`, `skills`, `questions`. |

## Shape wanted

- `packs//pack.json` for all 29, with `$schema` pointing at a `pack.schema.json`.
- Optional sibling code files, named from the JSON, only where needed: `detect.mjs` (3 packs), `env.mjs` (2), `contributed-rules.mjs` (1).
- Rules referenced **by filename**, which buys a drift guard the current shape cannot have: every rule `.mjs` in the pack directory must appear in exactly one of the two scope lists. Today an undeclared rule module is simply invisible.

## Why it is worth more than tidiness

**The loader stops executing arbitrary code at load.** Today a consumer's local `pack.mjs` is `import()`ed during SessionStart in every session and on every check run — which is precisely why `pack-registry.mjs` carries per-pack import isolation. With JSON, the ~26 packs that need no code execute none.

**A real schema.** `pack.schema.json` gives editor autocomplete and validation that `PACK_FIELDS` never will.

## What it costs

1. **The 350 comment lines have nowhere to go** — and they are real rationale, not noise: why `basics` requires `barriers` and contributes the isolation barrier as manifest data, why `canon-curation`'s declaration cardinality is what makes its tasks central-once. The natural home is the pack README, which is now exactly the "rationale the manifest cannot carry" file after #559 — this brings two or three of the deleted ones back.
2. **`pack.mjs` is a consumer-held shape**, not only ours — every member repo has local packs. Needs both-shapes tolerance plus a baseline migration to retire the old one, per `consumer-safe-changes.md`.

## Scope note on validation

A consumer's local pack must be validated at *their* Stop hook, not this repo's CI, so loader-side validation stays. ## What changed underneath it

1. **#827 settled the philosophy in this issue's favor, and further.** Declarative checks now live in `declared-checks.json` — JSON, one file per pack, discovered structurally with *no manifest line to keep in sync* — and the format's inability to hold comments was ruled a feature (enforcement by construction). The naming discipline from #789/#799/#800 (full-noun-phrase keys readable cold, no `description`/`doc` crutches) is the vocabulary standard any `detect` spec here must follow.
2. **The manifest vocabulary grew**: `version`/`minEngineVersion` (versioned updates), `seedOps`, validated `questions`, and the #555 split into `worldRules`/`workRules` — this issue predates all of them. Corpus today: **33 canon packs + the home's 2 local packs, 1362 lines, 49 imports**. `detect`: 17 functions / 16 null.
3. **The carrier problem now has real machinery.** When this was filed, "both-shapes tolerance plus a baseline migration" was hand-waving — the standing rule that a tightened member-owned contract must name its carrier came from the #555 incident (11 local packs rewritten by hand). Today: per-pack `migrations/` with version-gated fetch, and `applyStage: { why, instructions }` for member-side agentic work (the engine flow may never be agentic — versioned-updates DESIGN §5). The carrier for members' local `pack.mjs` files is therefore a **`basics` pack record** (declared everywhere, versioned — precedent: `2026-08-13-mechanism-versioned`), with `minEngineVersion` pinning the engine that reads the new shape.

## Revised code census

- **~10 detect functions are path-shaped one-liners** (basename-near-root, `endsWith`, `includes`, path regex) — pure data.
- **3 (jwt, web-speech, leaflet) are one regex over the content of path-filtered files** — also data, with a content-match key; the issue counted leaflet as "real logic" but the shape is uniform across the three.
- **3 genuinely code**: chrome-extension (`findExtensionManifest`), chrome-extension-release and static-website (both read constants out of their own rule modules). Sibling `detect.mjs` for these.
- `env` in 2 (node — functions of per-repo config; flutter), `contributes` in 5, `contributedRules` in 2 (barriers, canary-probe), `seedOps` in several.

## Decisions revised

- **"Rules referenced by filename" is half-superseded.** Declared checks are structural with no manifest line, *by design*. Coded rules should still be filename lists in `pack.json` — manifest placement stays the scope authority (#555), and the lists buy the drift guard: every `.mjs` at the pack root accounted for.
- **Schema enforcement route is the open call.** JSON Schema cannot carry the 20-word routing cap, skills↔tree agreement, or rule-scope agreement — so the code validator (`PACK_FIELDS`) survives in any variant. That argues for `pack.schema.json` as *editor tooling + documentation*, validated against the corpus and against `PACK_FIELDS` by canon-side drift tests, with the code validator remaining the single loader-side authority — rather than shipping a hand-rolled JSON-Schema interpreter in the dependency-free engine (PR #569's route).
- **The 350-comment-lines cost shrank.** #559's READMEs absorbed most of it (#569 measured this); what remains moves in the conversion.
- **Local packs get the versioned-update treatment**: canon converts wholesale (arrives via the ordinary mount converge, transactionally with the engine that reads it); members' local packs convert via the basics record's `applyStage`; the registry's `pack.mjs` tolerance retires when the record's `legacyPresent` telemetry reads clean fleet-wide, with a pinned expiry in a test per the live-cross-version-API discipline.

Migration plan follows as its own issue; PR #569 (built against the 2026-07-29 tree, pre-#555/pre-versions/pre-#827, and carrying the since-retired `agentic` migration field) gets a closing review separately.

declaration-and-configuration composition pattern packs use with each other, never a
   cross-pack code import (the canon-side `pack-independence` barrier) — universal via the
   baseline, with no per-project barriers config to maintain; its `gateDir` keeps it inert
   until the vendored mount exists, so it fires neither in the canon repo nor in pre-flip
   consumers.
9. **Migration notes v2.** A canon change that consumers must be amended for ships as a dated
   record (the `<flow>/migrations/<date>-<slug>/` shape): mechanical ops where code can
   express them, plus a **brief agentic note** for what it can't (chiefly adapting
   consumer-authored `local_packs/` content to a changed engine contract). The nightly applies
   the notes dated on or after the day of the repo's stamp (same-day inclusive, note
   idempotency absorbing the overlap — #330), oldest first, inside the one transactional commit.
   No read-side tolerances in live code, no `LEGACY_*` constants, and **no per-consumer state
   held in the canon** — the stamp in each consumer is the only bookkeeping. **Relevance is a
   fetch-time window, not a retention window**: records are kept forever, vendoring ships
   consumers only the notes landed within the last 7 days, and a repo lagging longer catches up
   from the fresh canon clone its baselining fetches, which carries every record. The one surviving two-phase case is
   **out-of-repo state** no commit can reach — the pasted web-environment Setup script keeps
   the probe + halt-gate pattern ([consumer-safe-changes.md](../consumer-safe-changes.md)).
10. **Accepted trade-off.** A bad canon change (typically an overzealous blocking check)
    reaches consumers on one nightly and its fix on a later one — up to ~two days' exposure.
    Dampers: the Stop hook's own two-block self-release, per-repo `rules`/`accept` overrides,
    and an on-demand refresh (the nightly's update step run in-session) as the
    pull-forward/emergency lane.

**What this retires:** the per-session fetch and its halt-gate, the `codeload.github.com`
allowlist prerequisite, `CLAUDINITE_REF` pinning (the commit *is* the pin), the
`.claudinite.new` swap and tracked-copy preservation, the Method A/B split with the submodule
caveats, and the stale-mount caveat in [engine/checks/README.md](../engine/checks/README.md). Session start
becomes a single offline SessionStart entry invoking [session-start.sh](../engine/hooks/session-start-command.sh)
directly (its steps are unchanged; a pack's own session-start step is fail-soft per 3, the env-check
halt-gate stays). The consumer `CLAUDE.md` carried nothing of Claudinite's — the corpus index,

content.text:
[{"id":5379959696,"body":"## Finding: the elimination premise does not survive contact with the files

I read every candidate site rather than working from the census summaries. **Close to none of the ~40–50 is safely eliminable.** The estimate in the issue body was derived from sweep summaries, which record *that* a pack asserts a GitHub fact but not *whether* the assertion is gratuitous. Reading them in context, almost every one is either already platform-neutral or load-bearing.

### Bucket 1 was largely a census artifact, not prose to fix

The sweeps counted the *concept* landing on Actions in practice, not GitHub vocabulary in the text. Checked line by line:

| Site | Text | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `firebase/skills/create-release-plan/SKILL.md:28,30` | "release-workflow variables", "the release workflow fails if any injected variable is unset" | already neutral |
| `macos/RULES.md:64,77` | "signing secrets being present", "in a build annotation" | already neutral |
| `spec-driven-product/RULES.md:56,127` | "gate the merge from CI", "cuts from `main`" | already neutral |
| `aws-sam/RULES.md:17` | "the last green deploy workflow" | already neutral |
| `web-scraping/RULES.md:59,154` | datacenter-IP blocks, commit-step durability | already neutral |
| `research-project/RULES.md:380` | "branch/commit/PR conventions" | cross-forge |

Genuine edits available: **1–2 marginal ones** (`firebase:50` "a workflow dispatch", `web-scraping:55` "repository secrets"), each worth one census point and each slightly *less* precise afterward. `macos/README.md:63` names GitHub Actions in a **provenance** note about a real project that genuinely used it — vaguening a factual attribution makes the doc worse, not more portable.

### Bucket 2: every candidate has a legitimate defense

- **Vendored stubs** (`chrome-extension`, `static-website` bump-version workflows) travel into member repos, where a canon reference dangles. Must stay self-contained.
- **Migration records** (`claudinite-fleet-sheepdog` ×2) are dated historical accounts. The canon says do not change historical records.
- **`task.md` files** (`claudinite-lifecycle`, `tidy-repo`, `jwt`, `product-wiki`) are read standalone by executor sessions.
- **The canary README** — the fact *is* the pack's reason to exist.
- **`claudinite-dashboard`** (`README.md:498`, `pack.mjs:37`) states the fact as the **premise** of a design decision (seed the workflow; follow the scheduler rather than `push`). It does not re-spell the withhold mechanism, and the canon rule permits A to say what it needs from B.
- **Squash-merge "restatements"** turned out not to exist: `basics` has none, and `tidy-repo/skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md:11` is a six-word parenthetical justifying its own decision rule.

### The always-loaded surface is already clean

`RULES.md` is the only text every session in every declaring repo pays for, and it is already lean: `tidy-repo/RULES.md` has **zero** GitHub mentions despite 11 credited assumptions (they live in skills and `task.mjs`, where they belong), and `basics/RULES.md`'s nine are the issue→branch→PR lifecycle itself, already delegating procedure to `git-github-advanced`.

### One genuinely ambiguous case, resolved against editing

`writing-tasks/SKILL.md:171` says `task.md` must state the **constraint** and drop the mechanism. The tracker cluster's "creation always lands an issue open and ignores a `state: closed` argument" is mechanism by that reading — but it is precisely what stops a session collapsing the two calls into one. Dropping it trades a census point for a live failure mode.

### Recommendation

**Do not run the sweep.** Landing ~40 edits to hit a number would vaguen accurate provenance, weaken standalone-readable task specs, and rewrite historical migration records — a net loss against a metric that was never a cost. The ~200 inherent assumptions are what these packs *do*; the only real lever is a forge-abstraction seam, which #959's standing decision rejects absent a second consumer.

[{"id":5379959696,"body":"## Finding: the elimination premise does not survive contact with the files

I read every candidate site rather than working from the census summaries. **Close to none of the ~40–50 is safely eliminable.** The estimate in the issue body was derived from sweep summaries, which record *that* a pack asserts a GitHub fact but not *whether* the assertion is gratuitous. Reading them in context, almost every one is either already platform-neutral or load-bearing.

### Bucket 1 was largely a census artifact, not prose to fix

The sweeps counted the *concept* landing on Actions in practice, not GitHub vocabulary in the text. Checked line by line:

| Site | Text | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `firebase/skills/create-release-plan/SKILL.md:28,30` | "release-workflow variables", "the release workflow fails if any injected variable is unset" | already neutral |
| `macos/RULES.md:64,77` | "signing secrets being present", "in a build annotation" | already neutral |
| `spec-driven-product/RULES.md:56,127` | "gate the merge from CI", "cuts from `main`" | already neutral |
| `aws-sam/RULES.md:17` | "the last green deploy workflow" | already neutral |
| `web-scraping/RULES.md:59,154` | datacenter-IP blocks, commit-step durability | already neutral |
| `research-project/RULES.md:380` | "branch/commit/PR conventions" | cross-forge |

Genuine edits available: **1–2 marginal ones** (`firebase:50` "a workflow dispatch", `web-scraping:55` "repository secrets"), each worth one census point and each slightly *less* precise afterward. `macos/README.md:63` names GitHub Actions in a **provenance** note about a real project that genuinely used it — vaguening a factual attribution makes the doc worse, not more portable.

### Bucket 2: every candidate has a legitimate defense

- **Vendored stubs** (`chrome-extension`, `static-website` bump-version workflows) travel into member repos, where a canon reference dangles. Must stay self-contained.
- **Migration records** (`claudinite-fleet-sheepdog` ×2) are dated historical accounts. The canon says do not change historical records.
- **`task.md` files** (`claudinite-lifecycle`, `tidy-repo`, `jwt`, `product-wiki`) are read standalone by executor sessions.
- **The canary README** — the fact *is* the pack's reason to exist.
- **`claudinite-dashboard`** (`README.md:498`, `pack.mjs:37`) states the fact as the **premise** of a design decision (seed the workflow; follow the scheduler rather than `push`). It does not re-spell the withhold mechanism, and the canon rule permits A to say what it needs from B.
- **Squash-merge "restatements"** turned out not to exist: `basics` has none, and `tidy-repo/skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md:11` is a six-word parenthetical justifying its own decision rule.

### The always-loaded surface is already clean

`RULES.md` is the only text every session in every declaring repo pays for, and it is already lean: `tidy-repo/RULES.md` has **zero** GitHub mentions despite 11 credited assumptions (they live in skills and `task.mjs`, where they belong), and `basics/RULES.md`'s nine are the issue→branch→PR lifecycle itself, already delegating procedure to `git-github-advanced`.

### One genuinely ambiguous case, resolved against editing

`writing-tasks/SKILL.md:171` says `task.md` must state the **constraint** and drop the mechanism. The tracker cluster's "creation always lands an issue open and ignores a `state: closed` argument" is mechanism by that reading — but it is precisely what stops a session collapsing the two calls into one. Dropping it trades a census point for a live failure mode.

### Recommendation

**Do not run the sweep.** Landing ~40 edits to hit a number would vaguen accurate provenance, weaken standalone-readable task specs, and rewrite historical migration records — a net loss against a metric that was never a cost. The ~200 inherent assumptions are what these packs *do*; the only real lever is a forge-abstraction seam, which #959's standing decision rejects absent a second consumer.

No code changes pushed. Awaiting a decision on whether to close this as not-planned.
